newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia quiet after weekend campaign violence.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia quiet after weekend campaign violence.

text.p: Calm returned on Monday to areas of Indonesia's main island of Java, which was hit by a fresh bout of pre-election violence between rival political groups over the weekend, the national police said.
"From the view of the national police, it's safe and under control," national police spokesman Brigadier-General Nurfaizi told Reuters in Jakarta.

Supporters of the ruling Golkar and the minority Moslem-oriented United Development Party (PPP) clashed in major centres on Java, including the capital Jakarta and the ancient city of Yogyakarta on the final weekend of campaigning before the May 29 elections.
The campaign ends on May 23, followed by a cooling-off period before the vote.

Despite the confrontations, with thousands of supporters of the two parties hurling stones and other projectiles at each other as police and troops moved to keep them apart, there were no immediate reports of casualties or arrests.
Shops and businesses were open on Monday and streets were jammed with traffic as usual.
"There is nothing to worry about as the situation has been controlled and the activities of the community can continue as usual," Nurfaizi said.

Financial markets were cautious following the violence, with Jakarta stocks closing down 0.69 percent at 652.55 points, but dealers and brokers said share-price movements were within acceptable limits.

"We see it very much as a very, very short term impact, and really as of next Friday (when the campaign ends) all bets are on again," said Stephen Doe, director of research with Asia Equities Jasereh brokerage.

The only other party legally entitled to contest the election, the Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI), was campaigning on Java on Monday. But the party has been badly split since the ouster of its former leader Megawati Sukarnoputri last year and has been drawing mediocre support.
The three parties issued a statement on Sunday night saying they would halt all mass public rallies in Jakarta for the rest of the campaign.
The country's powerful military said the violence was part of a plot to topple long-ruling President Suharto and blamed radicals who it said were linked to the banned Indonesian Communist Party.
Political analysts said authorities routinely blamed radicals for violence and any failings in the country's system.
Some 125 million people in the world's fourth most populous nation will be eligible to vote in the election.
Golkar's platform stresses social and economic development, while the other parties are emphasising a drive against corruption and the need for more open democracy.
In the town of Bantul south of Yogyakarta, Suharto's eldest daughter Siti Hardianti Rukmana, also known as Tutut, appeared in public with the country's best-known Moslem leader on Sunday.
"Tutut is a future leader," said Abdurrahman Wahid, the leader of the non-political Nahadlatul Ulama (NU), which claims 30 million members.

"Thank God that Tutut has something in common with NU, at least when it comes to promoting unity. We believe Tutut will bring the rythmn of unity," he added after the meeting between Rukmana and local Moslem leaders.
Although Indonesian law prohibits election appeals based on religion, Rukmana said her public meeting was within the rules.
"It is not only Golkar which tries to woo the NU...I think the case is the same for PPP and PDI. But it depends on them (which to choose)," she told reporters.
